chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Crises of the 21st Century

lessons.title: The 2013 Taper Tantrum: How the US Fed Shook the Rupee

body.text: In 2013, the US Federal Reserve did not raise rates, sell a single bond or cut its stimulus. It only hinted that it might slow down. That hint alone was enough to send the rupee to a record low.

children.text: On 22 May 2013, Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke told the US Congress that if the economy kept improving, the Fed could, "in the next few meetings, take a step down in our pace of purchases." The Fed was buying $85 billion of bonds every month at the time. Bernanke's comment was carefully hedged, but markets heard only one thing: the flood of cheap dollars was going to slow.

Within three months, foreign investors had pulled billions out of Indian bonds, and on 28 August 2013 the rupee hit ₹68.85 per dollar. India was not in a banking crisis and had not defaulted on anything. This lesson explains why a speech in Washington hit India so hard, and how the RBI fought back.

body.caption: The taper tantrum on the five-stage map

cells: Build-up
Years of near-zero US rates and Fed bond buying push cheap money into emerging markets, while India runs a record current account deficit
Trigger
Bernanke's 22 May 2013 hint that the Fed could slow its bond purchases
Panic and recognition
Foreign investors sell Indian bonds, the rupee falls to ₹68.85, and India is grouped with the "Fragile Five"
Policy response
The RBI tightens liquidity, the government curbs gold imports, and new Governor Raghuram Rajan opens a special dollar swap window
Repair and recovery
Dollar inflows rebuild reserves, the current account deficit shrinks, and India builds much larger buffers in the years that follow

children.text: Build-up: A Flood of Cheap Dollars
After 2008, the Fed cut its policy rate to near zero. When that was not enough, it began
quantitative easing
, buying bonds on a massive scale. By 2013, it was buying $85 billion a month.

markDefs.definition: A central bank creating money to buy large amounts of government bonds and other securities, pushing long-term interest rates down to support borrowing, spending and asset prices.

children.text: With US yields so low, global investors went looking for better returns. Indian government bonds paying around 8% looked very attractive, so money flowed in. But that money came with a condition: it would stay only as long as the extra yield was worth the currency risk.
The slowing of QE purchases became known as the
taper
. The sudden market reaction to the mere idea of it became the taper tantrum.

markDefs.definition: The gradual reduction of a central bank's bond purchases under quantitative easing. Tapering is not tightening yet; it means adding stimulus more slowly.

body.latex: \text{Foreign investor's return in \$} = (1 + \text{Rupee yield}) \times \frac{\text{Rupee rate at entry}}{\text{Rupee rate at exit}} - 1
body.caption: Rupee rates are quoted as rupees per dollar. A higher exit rate means a weaker rupee and a lower dollar return.

body.title: Find the Breakeven Rupee
body.prompt: A foreign investor buys an Indian government bond yielding 8% a year when the rupee is at ₹55 per dollar. Ignoring price changes on the bond, at what rupee rate one year later would the investor earn exactly zero return in dollars? Give your answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Set the dollar return to zero: 1.08 × 55 ÷ exit rate = 1, so the exit rate = 1.08 × 55 = ₹59.4. If the rupee weakens beyond ₹59.4 per dollar, the whole 8% yield is wiped out in dollar terms. In 2013, the rupee went to ₹68.85. Once investors expected that kind of move, selling first became the rational choice.

children.text: Why India Was Hit Harder Than Most
Every emerging market felt the tantrum, but India was among the worst hit because it had borrowed its way into the same weaknesses you saw in 1991, only milder.

cells: Record current account deficit
4.8% of GDP in 2012-13, and 6.7% in October to December 2012
India needed large foreign inflows every quarter just to pay its bills abroad
Heavy gold imports
A rising share of India's import bill
Gold buying added to the deficit without adding to productive capacity
Reliance on portfolio money
Foreign holdings of Indian bonds at $38.52 billion in May 2013
Bond investors can sell and leave in days
High inflation and slowing growth
Limited room to cut or raise rates freely
The RBI faced a stagflation-style dilemma, as in the 1970s

body.text: Chapter 1 described the wake-up call channel through the "Fragile Five" label. This lesson shows the mechanics underneath it: a country that depends on foreign money to fund a big current account deficit is only as stable as that money's patience.

events.title: Bernanke's hint
events.description: The Fed chairman says the Fed could take a step down in its bond purchases in the next few meetings. Foreign holdings of Indian bonds had just peaked at $38.52 billion.

events.title: The selling spreads
events.description: After the Fed's June meeting spells out a possible timetable, US yields climb further and emerging market bonds and currencies slide.

events.title: The RBI tightens
events.description: The RBI raises its Marginal Standing Facility rate to 10.25%, three percentage points above the repo rate of 7.25%, and caps banks' borrowing from it, making it costlier to bet against the rupee.

events.title: The "Fragile Five"
events.description: A Morgan Stanley analyst groups India with Brazil, Indonesia, South Africa and Turkey as the most vulnerable emerging markets.

events.title: Rupee hits ₹68.85
events.description: The rupee falls 3.7% in a single day to a record low against the dollar.

events.title: Rajan takes charge
events.description: On his first day as RBI Governor, Raghuram Rajan announces a special swap window for banks' foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians.

events.title: US yields peak for the year
events.description: The US 10-year Treasury yield reaches 2.96%, up from 1.94% before Bernanke's testimony.

events.title: The Fed surprises
events.description: The Fed decides not to taper yet, catching markets off guard and giving emerging markets breathing room.

events.title: Dollars flow back in
events.description: Banks raise nearly $34 billion through the swap window, about $27 billion of it through FCNR(B) deposits.

events.title: The taper finally arrives
events.description: The Fed announces it will cut monthly purchases from $85 billion to $75 billion from January 2014. Markets, now prepared, take it calmly.

children.text: Policy Response: How India Fought Back

India did not have a simple way out. Raising interest rates sharply would defend the rupee but hurt an economy that was already slowing. Letting the rupee fall freely risked panic and imported inflation. The episode is a textbook example of the
impossible trinity

markDefs.definition: The idea that a country cannot have all three at once: a fixed or stable exchange rate, free movement of capital, and an independent interest rate policy. It must give up at least one.

body.title: Go deeper: the impossible trinity in 2013

children.text: A country can pick only two of these three goals at the same time.

cells: Stable exchange rate and free capital flows
Independent interest rates
Hong Kong, whose peg to the dollar means its rates follow US rates
Free capital flows and independent interest rates
A stable exchange rate
Countries with freely floating currencies
Stable exchange rate and independent interest rates
Free capital flows

children.text: In 2013, India had opened its bond market to foreign money and wanted to set rates for its own economy, so pressure fell on the rupee. To steady it, the RBI temporarily bent its interest rate policy by tightening short-term rates in July, and the government leaned on controls such as gold import curbs. Every tool had a cost. There was no free option.

cells: Tighter liquidity
The Marginal Standing Facility rate raised to 10.25%, and bank borrowing from the RBI capped, in July 2013
Make borrowing rupees to buy dollars expensive
Gold import curbs
Import duty on gold raised in stages to 10%, and the 80:20 rule requiring 20% of imported gold to be exported
Cut the current account deficit
A new dollar source
A special RBI swap window for FCNR(B) deposits from non-resident Indians, opened 4 September 2013
Bring in stable dollars quickly

body.label: Diaspora Dollars, Again
body.context: By offering banks a concessional rate to swap foreign currency deposits into rupees, the RBI made it attractive for non-resident Indians to park dollars in Indian banks for three years. Banks raised nearly $34 billion in total through the window. It is the same idea as the Resurgent India Bonds of 1998: when hot money leaves, turn to the diaspora.

body.title: Why Tighten in a Slowdown?
body.question: India's growth was slowing in mid-2013, which would normally call for lower interest rates. Why did the RBI push short-term rates up in July 2013?
options: To fight a stock market bubble
To make it more expensive to borrow rupees and bet against the currency, steadying the rupee as foreign money left
Because the US Fed had already raised its rates
To encourage banks to lend more to businesses
body.explanation: The RBI was defending the rupee. Speculators and importers rushing to buy dollars needed rupees to do it, so making short-term rupee funding expensive slowed the selling. The Fed had not raised rates at all, only hinted at slowing its bond purchases. This is the impossible trinity in action: with capital flowing freely, protecting the currency forced the RBI to set rates for the rupee, not for growth.

body.title: Name the Policy
body.textWithBlank: When a central bank creates money to buy bonds on a massive scale to push long-term interest rates down, it is called quantitative ___.
body.explanation: Quantitative easing, or QE. The taper tantrum was a reaction to the Fed signalling it would slow its QE purchases, not to any actual rate hike.

children.text: Repair: Building Buffers for Next Time

The tantrum passed. The Fed tapered from January 2014 without another panic, and India's current account deficit narrowed as gold imports fell. The deeper lesson for the RBI was that reserves and a small current account deficit are the best defence against global money turning away. India's foreign exchange reserves reached a record $785.71 billion in the week of 4 September 2026, a very different position from 2013.

body.title: The Fed Talks Tough Again
body.scenario: Imagine the US Fed unexpectedly signals that US interest rates will stay high for much longer than markets expected. US bond yields jump. You have money in three places: an Indian gilt fund, shares of a large Indian IT services exporter, and shares of an airline that buys fuel priced in dollars.
body.prompt: Using the lessons of 2013, explain how each holding might be affected in the short term, and what would make India more or less vulnerable this time.
body.modelAnswer: Gilt fund: higher US yields make Indian bonds relatively less attractive, so foreign investors may sell. Indian bond yields could rise and prices fall, pulling the fund's NAV down in the short term, as happened in 2013 when India's 10-year yield rose. IT exporter: a weaker rupee raises the rupee value of its dollar revenues, which tends to support earnings, although a slowdown in US demand could offset some of this. Airline: a weaker rupee raises the rupee cost of fuel and aircraft leases, both linked to the dollar, squeezing margins, so it is typically among the hardest hit. What would make India less vulnerable than in 2013: much larger forex reserves, a smaller current account deficit, and a proven RBI toolkit including intervention in currency markets. What would make it more vulnerable: a large current account deficit returning, heavy dependence on foreign portfolio money in Indian bonds, especially after Indian bonds entered global bond indices, and high inflation limiting the RBI's room to act. The core lesson of 2013 is to watch the current account deficit and the stickiness of foreign money, not just the headline from the Fed.
